content: 1. Investigate the impact of indeterminate, non-determinate, or invalid diagnostic results on the accuracy of tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis and patient outcomes. 2. Evaluate the use of low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for initial TB detection in all individuals presenting with TB symptoms, including children and people living with HIV. Assess their utility as follow-on tests and compare the interpretation of high-complexity hybridization-based NAAT results with sequencing and emerging evidence on genotypic and phenotypic associations. 3. Conduct rigorous studies on loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis, using high-quality reference standards and diverse specimen types, including extrapulmonary samples, to improve specificity estimates. 4. Determine training requirements, assess competency, and ensure quality assurance for TB-LAMP implementation. 5. Study the impact of TB-LAMP on TB treatment initiation, morbidity, and mortality. 6. Perform cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit analyses of targeted TB-LAMP use in specific countries. 7. Use the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) to enhance the quality of diagnostic research reporting. 8. Improve understanding of the correlation between resistance-conferring mutations detected by follow-on NAATs, culture-based drug susceptibility testing, and patient outcomes. 9. Review evidence to confirm or revise critical concentrations used in culture-based drug susceptibility testing. 10. Investigate the correlation between specific mutations detected by follow-on NAATs and the minimum inhibitory concentrations of individual drugs. 11. Determine the detection limits of follow-on NAATs for heteroresistance. 12. Collect evidence on the mortality impact of initiating appropriate treatment for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 13. Conduct cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit analyses of follow-on NAATs in specific countries. 14. Conduct clinical trials to assess the impact of targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) on patient outcomes. 15. Evaluate the accuracy and effectiveness of targeted NGS for detecting resistance to new and repurposed drugs, such as pretomanid, across diverse geographic and epidemiologic settings. 16. Undertake qualitative and quantitative research to understand the perspectives of end-users and clinicians regarding the acceptability and feasibility of targeted NGS. 17. Develop and evaluate effective implementation models for integrating targeted NGS into laboratory networks, optimizing algorithms to improve timely access to testing, treatment initiation, and patient outcomes. 18. Develop strategies to enhance the efficiency of targeted NGS testing, including sample processing, bacterial load thresholds, and molecular transport mediums for sample storage and transfer. 19. Map sequencing capacity within countries and optimize diagnostic networks to ensure cross-disciplinary use of sequencing machines and shared costs. 20. Regularly monitor performance data, including resistance rates, turnaround times, and sequencing quality metrics, while participating in external quality assurance programs. 21. Integrate sequencing data into existing surveillance systems to monitor drug resistance trends and update the WHO mutation catalog. 22. Collect cost data to address questions about scaling up targeted NGS, balancing turnaround time with batching, and optimizing cost-effectiveness in various settings. 23. Evaluate the impact of multi-disease testing on program operations, costs, and resource requirements. 24. Assess the time to treatment initiation, treatment outcomes, and cost-effectiveness of targeted NGS implementation. 25. Develop or optimize diagnostic tests to improve performance and predictive value for measuring progression to active TB. 26. Compare the effectiveness of fixed-dose combination TB treatments with separate drug formulations in patients with drug-susceptible TB. 27. Conduct pharmacokinetic studies to evaluate the bioavailability of fixed-dose combinations and separate drug formulations, and develop better weight-banding categories for drug dosing. 28. Establish the optimal dose of rifampicin in different drug formulations for all age groups. 29. Investigate the effects of steroids in TB meningitis, including optimal dosing, duration, and differences based on HIV status or antiretroviral therapy use. 30. Study the relationship between steroid treatment and cancer risk. 31. Evaluate the efficacy of a four-month regimen of isoniazid, rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, including its use in extrapulmonary TB and specific subgroups such as children, pregnant women, and people with HIV. 32. Investigate the acquisition of drug resistance during treatment with the four-month regimen. 33. Assess the cost-effectiveness, equity impact, and patient acceptability of the shorter four-month regimen. 34. Study the use of fixed-dose combination formulations for the shorter regimen to reduce pill burden. 35. Conduct operational research on the advantages of directly observed treatment versus self-administered therapy. 36. Monitor treatment adherence, completion, and outcomes in operational settings. 37. Conduct randomized controlled trials to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of regimens for isoniazid-resistant TB, including cases with additional resistance to other drugs. 38. Investigate the potential benefits and risks of high-dose isoniazid treatment. 39. Optimize the composition and duration of regimens for children and adults with isoniazid-resistant TB, particularly high-dose isoniazid and second-line medicines. 40. Assess the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of the six-month BPaLM/BPaL regimen for MDR/RR-TB and pre-extensively drug-resistant TB across diverse populations, including children, pregnant women, and people with HIV. 41. Identify mechanisms and molecular markers of pretomanid resistance and monitor resistance development. 42. Record and analyze adverse events associated with pretomanid, focusing on hepatotoxicity and reproductive toxicity. 43. Investigate the efficacy of pretomanid and delamanid in multidrug regimens and their potential cross-resistance. 44. Explore opportunities to optimize the BPaLM regimen by replacing moxifloxacin with levofloxacin. 45. Monitor resistance to new and repurposed medicines and investigate cross-resistance between bedaquiline and clofazimine. 46. Conduct research on the safety, efficacy, and tolerability of all-oral shorter MDR-TB treatment regimens compared to longer regimens. 47. Identify optimal companion drugs to protect bedaquiline and limit resistance acquisition, considering its long half-life and potential single-drug exposure. 48. Optimize regimen composition when new-generation medicines become available and evaluate the efficacy of other six-month regimens.
